Ex-Overwatch director Jeff Kaplan ignores everything about the hero shooter after his 'almost clinical' departure 5 years ago: 'I don't search for my name in Overwatch. I don't search for Overwatch. I sort of just disconnect.'
summary: The former Blizzard developer has moved on.
body: Despite some big changes happening with Overwatch lately, former game director Jeff Kaplan hasn't touched it since the year he left Blizzard. In fact, he actively avoids the game in every way he can, he told GameSpot in a recent interview. Before Overwatch, Kaplan rose through the ranks on the World of Warcraft team, starting in QA and eventually becoming game director. He described his departure from the WoW team in 2008 as "a training moment" for when he would leave the Overwatch team, and Blizzard altogether, in 2021. "I kind of went through a little bit of shock leaving WoW back in 2008," Kaplan says. "So, when I stepped away from Overwatch in April of 2021, I was kind of used to that moment of what it meant to give all of yourself, your heart, your soul–because it's not just a job, there's no one who can do this and have it just be a job–and then have this shocking moment where you realize it doesn't belong to you. It belongs to the team, belongs to the players, it belongs to Blizzard, but it doesn’t belong to you." Kaplan says he "had a very almost clinical separation" with Overwatch after what he went through with WoW. As a result, he stopped playing it the moment he left a…

title: Looking back on 10 years of Overwatch, the promises kept, and where Team 4 goes from here
summary: "In order for people to play the game in the present, they need to have confidence in its future."
body: 10 years is a long time for anything, but for a live service game it's a milestone that very few are able to cross. Overwatch made it over the line earlier this year, and has since been able to do something of a victory lap because after all the highs and the lows, Overwatch is in the best place it's ever been . "It doesn't feel like 10 years to me," game director Aaron Keller tells me. "Although, I could probably answer that question in a few ways. There's probably a year or two that might have felt like five or six years in the middle of this process, but there's always so much to be doing on the team and for the game." But Keller reiterates the good old adage "if you love what you do, you never work a day in your life. (Image credit: Blizzard) "Our team is filled with people that are not just passionate about making games, they're passionate about Overwatch itself, our heroes and the world in which they reside. So when you get to go into the office and talk about that all day, the time can fly by pretty quickly." title: Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced was a big hit, and now it's time for big layoffs at the studio that made it
summary: Ubisoft has also decided to close Trials studio Ubisoft Redlynx entirely.
body: Three months after the very successful launch of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced , a game that sold two million copies in a single day ( three million copies in a week!) and surpassed "annual expectations" in just two weeks, Ubisoft has laid off 70 people from developer Ubisoft Singapore. In a statement provided to PC Gamer, the publisher also said it plans to close the Ubisoft Redlynx studio outright. This would be reason number two on our list of 25 foolproof ways to get laid off in the videogame industry: Make a game that sells so well, it blows away all expectations and makes even more money than anyone dared hope. Of course, we've already seen this in play with Black Flag Resynced—Ubisoft Barcelona, a support studio on the game, had nearly a third of its number cut shortly after it launched. The Ubisoft Barcelona layoffs might seem particularly egregious, coming so soon after it produced a much-needed win for a publisher that's spent the past few years taking big Ls , but it's not the only bad news. A year after announcing a " restructuring proposal " for Ubisoft Redlynx aimed at reducing costs and ensuring "a stronger prioritization and efficiency across the company’s w…

title: If New Blood had made Dusk 2, there'd be no Iron Lung, 'and now David Szymanski has got a movie that made $50 million'—so maybe there's wisdom in not churning out sequels
summary: You don't need to milk your cash cows.
body: New Blood boss Dave Oshry isn't interested in running a massive studio that follows the blockbuster strategy of milking its successful games for all they're worth. The publisher-developer combo has enjoyed a string of big wins with its boomer shooters, but Oshry's plan for building on success is to invest that money into new projects. "I think a lot of studios would have a big hit like Ultrakill ," Oshry tells us, "and then they would maybe open a big office, or just milk the shit out of Ultrakill and do Ultrakill spinoffs, or use that money to make sequels. And I've decided to put that money into projects like Gloomwood and Fallen Aces , artsy projects like Tenebris Somnia . That’s what I've decided to do with our success because I can, because we're independent." The goal, says Oshry, has never been to create "a big studio with an office and hundreds of employees … I don't know why anyone would want that". And thankfully he doesn't have to deal with shareholders and investors telling him to just keep milking and keep growing. "The fact that we're one studio and that I control everything means that I can make those kinds of decisions," he says. "If we had publishers or shareholde…

title: Fortnite is coming to Linux once Epic improves Easy Anti-Cheat
summary: A major shooter is pushing past the Linux anticheat barrier.
body: Epic intends to launch Fortnite on Linux, but first, it's "rebuilding Easy Anti-Cheat" to support the move. "Once [EAC Linux v2 is] working with a critical mass of distro maintainers, we'll bring Fortnite to Linux via the Epic Games Launcher," the company announced. "We'll also make these improvements available to other developers so they can bring their games to Linux players." More PC games than ever are playable on Linux, thanks in part to Valve's Proton emulation, which allows many Windows games to be played on SteamOS and has been essential to the Steam Deck's success. But some of the biggest multiplayer games have been holdouts, because opening the doors to Linux represents a security and cheating risk. For example, former Facepunch COO Alistair McFarlane said last year that the studio's popular survival game, Rust, was unsupported on Linux because of cheating. "There are no plans to support Proton or Linux," McFarlane said at the time. "It's a vector for cheat developers, and one that would be poorly maintained by both us and EAC due to the low user base. When we stopped support for Linux, we saw more cheat users exploiting Linux, than actual legitimate users." Epic's move …

title: GTA 6 was delayed partially because the amount of NPCs was 'horrifying' and required a dedicated studio full of writers to handle
summary: "We [could have] hit that schedule, but it won’t be the game we want to make."
body: Grand Theft Auto 6 , originally slated to be released back in May, was delayed to November —the reason given at the time was "to finish the game with the level of polish you have come to expect and deserve". And while that still very much holds true, the reality of the game's scope and stature was apparently kinda terrifying from a production standpoint. Speaking with Bloomberg , co-head of development Rob Nelson commented on one reason for the delay—the amount of NPCs that were required to populate Leonida: "The projections they were giving us were horrifying." The solution? A kind of NPC emergency room, an entire studio set up in LA solely designed to handle the workload. Another development co-head, Phil Hooker, comments: "I think when it became apparent that some areas weren’t going to make it, that’s when we decided to make the shift of date. We could hit that schedule, but it won’t be the game we want to make." Being perfectly candid, for a moment: This fills me both with a sense of dread and relief. title: I just tricked DLSS into running on my AMD GPU in Cyberpunk 2077 and Alan Wake 2 and all it took was running a single script
summary: It's easy enough to install, so worth a try, I'd say.
body: If you have an older AMD card, you might want to take a look at a new, easy-to-use tool that allows you to use DLSS rather than FSR 3. I've been trying it out, and it works really well and is easy to install. The tool, HelixSR , works by making patched games believe they're still running FSR 3.1, but it replaces the upscaling algorithm with DLSS 3.7 (Model E). It bases the new upscaling DLL file it hands the game on the official DLSS one. The upscaling is done using your regular shader cores, of course, given there aren't Tensor cores to make use of in your AMD GPU. This being said, the differences in image quality are very far from night and day, and dropping in the DLSS patch actually decreases performance very slightly. I'd still say the tool is worth a try. If worst comes to worst, you can uninstall it by running a simple pre-packaged script. AMD has come a long way since the time when its upscaling solution was far behind Nvidia's, both in terms of game support and quality. Now, so many games support FSR 4 that I can't justify taking the time to count them like I used to when I wrote about it, and image quality isn't too far behind Nvidia. But much of this depends on which ve…

The Index VR headset launched in 2019 for $499, but now you can get one for $399.20. Keep in mind that the Index VR headset doesn't come with controllers or a base station. A package bundling those used to cost $999, but that option is no longer available and thus, there's no associated discount. Left controller replacements and replacement tethers are going for $119.20 and $103.20 respectively. No, there aren't any right controller replacements listed. It seems that if you want controllers for your Index VR, you'll probably need to buy them elsewhere. The same goes for base stations. "Valve Index is no longer being produced," reads a Steam news item published earlier today. "Remaining Index headsets, controllers, and accessories are still available at the new prices below while supplies last." That "while supplies last" is crucial: obviously Valve won't be making any more, and they've given no sense of how many they have lying around. "I wasn’t particularly interested at first, but since it’s Zach Cregger’s latest film, I went to see Resident Evil," Kojima posted on Twitter on October 12. "Right from the opening, it hits you with music reminiscent of "The Thing." From there, it’s a relentless barrage of classic horror techniques, terrifying situations, and jump scares that never lets up until the very end." That bit is sorta why I said seemingly above. Do I detect a little backhanded praise? Calling it a "relentless barrage" isn't necessarily a compliment, saying a director used "classic horror techniques" could be a way of saying it's unoriginal, and pointing out that there are "jump scares" throughout might suggest it's not a particularly sophisticated film. You'll find the seal of an emissary from Bonaparte in an abandoned carriage, but the quest will indicate you somehow need to get through the clouds of poison infesting the camp to progress it further. title: I was excited by Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons until the protagonist pulled out a sword
summary: Can't we just stick to the magic?
body: Considering only eight minutes of it were shown at Gamescom's Opening Night Live, I went on a real journey with Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons . At first, I was nonplussed by it. While the production values were impressive, it also looked like every Sony game released in the last ten years, right down to the specific angle of the camera and the quippy NPC companion. Yet as the reveal unfurled, I found myself growing intrigued by Warlock's invocation-based puzzle-solving and combat. Levitating objects to create platforms, using teleportation spells to swap places with enemies, conjuring a whole-ass storm to make electrical attacks more viable. It's rare to see a game of this scope encourage guile and cleverness from the player, to set its mechanical ambitions slightly beyond timed dodges and grisly executions. (Image credit: Wizards of the Coast) And then, just as I thought I was sold on Warlock, the main character pulled out a sword. Well, to be specific, Warlock's magical protagonist Kaatri conjured a sword. After all, why bother lugging around several pounds of sharpened steel when you can just make one appear out of thin air any time you like? It's silly to carry around a sword th…

title: Ben Affleck lost 3 years to Starcraft, has strong Valorant opinions, and mourns RTSes as a genre, so there's solid odds he's one of our regular commenters
summary: He's also handsome and wealthy. I'm beginning to think we're the same guy.
body: Unlike PC Gamer's UK editorial staff , Ben Affleck knows ball. Metaphorically, I mean. Though he probably also knows what the Miami Heat is. Speaking on the October 12 episode of the Happy Sad Confused podcast , Affleck reflected—with a touch of regret—on the time Starcraft swallowed his entire life. "There was a game called Starcraft that probably took the most life out of me for a period of time. I had just gotten famous, and all I did was stay home for three years and play Starcraft." The celebs, folks—they're just like us. More so than usual in Affleck's case, I suppose, since the actor's videogame career doesn't only encompass a brief dalliance with Blizzard's RTS series. "Valorant's a great game. It's a great game," he continued, "The problem with that game is that—the kids that have been raised playing, I just get fuckin' rocked. I'm like, 'Are you mother fuckers cheating?' And I get mad. And they're like 11, they're like, 'Fuck you loser!' It's very humiliating, but that's a great game." title: Hundreds of layoffs and many cancelled projects later, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma reportedly says 'we will not survive' without new IPs

body: Thousands of layoffs , a couple of booted studios, and a re-organisation of Obsidian away from its newer projects and onto Fallout later, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has reportedly taken to an internal town hall and talked about the importance of new IP. The transcript, as shared by Windows Central , goes as follows: "We're backing our strongest franchises. I want our great games to become great global billion-dollar franchises. I would also like to see us continue to create enduring new IP. We will not survive if we only revive [sic] on the past. We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP, that reaches new sets of audiences." This is, to put it gently, very confusing. As part of Xbox's "Reset", the studio has done the following: Cancelled multiple projects from Obsidian and told it to go make a Fallout game . Made Double Fine go independent . Did the same to South of Midnight studio Compulsion Games . Put its sights on Arkane Lyon . Is, at present, in consultation talks regarding Ninja Theory after attempted sales failed.
